sourceScope: Sources motivate dimensions and broad techniques. Entry definitions, labels, signals, exact mappings and bounds are original Awen proposals, not validated ontology or classifier.

sources.title: Emotional expression in music: contribution, linearity, and additivity of primary musical cues
sources.observation: Manipulated musical cues affect perceived emotional character in the tested excerpts. The study distinguishes cue dimensions; it does not validate narrative labels or reading benefit.

sources.title: Emotions evoked by the sound of music
sources.observation: Music-related emotion measurement distinguishes perceived and felt response and varies with musical preference. This is not a paragraph ontology or an enjoyment reward for reading.

sources.title: Perspective - Point of View
sources.observation: Narrative presentation depends on narrator or character position and values. Awen must record whose experience is represented rather than assume one objective emotion.

sources.title: Human brain activity time-locked to narrative event boundaries
sources.observation: Readers segment brief narratives at situation changes, including character goals. This motivates contextual boundary annotations, not musical resets at every paragraph.

sources.title: The Semantic Evolution of Chromatic Mediants
sources.observation: Treats mediant associations as historically conventional; its film example shows magical harmony supporting comic mockery.

sources.title: Interview with Chris Houston
sources.reviewed: Questions on composition, script spotting and underscoring
sources.observation: Describes reducing melody around theatrical speech and adapting music to script, period and production; this is one practitioner account.

sources.title: Awen work-specific classical source review
sources.reviewed: Previously scoped Bach/Vivaldi/Chopin references; source claims remain in their original records
sources.observation: Programme and analysis evidence is section-specific. Seasonal/environment mappings below are Awen alternatives, not universal emotions or new score analysis.

musicalOptions.rationale: Keep comic motion light rather than maximise threat.
Test short articulated movement at the existing 72 BPM clock.
Test held harmony and space instead of constant escalation.
Retain a small figure while preserving tonal identity.
Connected figuration offers discovery without a large harmonic surprise.
Test a more noticeable harmonic colour only at a permitted boundary.
Leave upper-line gaps; the theatre analogy is a reading hypothesis.
Reflection can keep gentle motion and need not sound sorrowful.
A sparse repeated gesture is one possible treatment of loss.
A held spacious alternative for safety, intimacy or aftermath.
Separated calls offer one landscape treatment; setting alone does not determine mood.
Dry repeated articulation is a programme-inspired cold alternative, not winter equals sadness.

entries.definition: An agent actively chases, escapes or evades an obstacle now.

examples.positive: She raced for the exit as the guards followed.
examples.counter: He recalled a chase from childhood.

cues.context: Require an actual event and direction; distinguish a metaphor or quoted plan.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Waiting or preparation whose outcome remains unresolved.

examples.positive: They waited for the latch to move.
examples.counter: The door had already opened and the danger passed.

cues.context: Stillness can coexist with high threat; do not infer low activation from waiting.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: An active opposition, collision or decisive encounter.

examples.positive: The two rivals blocked each other at the gate.
examples.counter: She wondered whether they might meet.

cues.context: Separate actual impact from a possible future encounter.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: New information changes a character or narrator understanding.

examples.positive: Only then did she understand who had sent the letter.
examples.counter: She repeated what everyone already knew.

cues.context: Distinguish revelation from a neutral visual description.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: An exchange, explanation or verbal negotiation occupies the scene.

examples.positive: He asked; she answered quietly.
examples.counter: No one said a word as they ran.

cues.context: A speech verb may frame recalled action; dialogue may also contain threat or humour.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: A pause in outward action develops thought, memory or evaluation.

examples.positive: She considered what the promise meant.
examples.counter: She sprinted without time to think.

cues.context: Reflection is a function, not a synonym for sadness or low stakes.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: The consequences after an event become the main focus.

examples.positive: After the struggle they counted the missing.
examples.counter: The struggle was about to begin.

cues.context: A temporal link must establish the preceding event; dust alone may be scenery.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Concealment, planning or manoeuvring with incomplete information.

examples.positive: He hid the key and gave a deliberately false name.
examples.counter: He plainly introduced himself.

cues.context: Do not equate every unknown detail with deception.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Rapid or effortful activity is established in this passage.

examples.positive: They scrambled across the falling bridge.
examples.counter: The word run appeared on the old sign.

cues.context: Activation and emotional valence are independent; humour and danger can both be active.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Movement or outward activity is sparse or sustained.

examples.positive: They sat beside the fire and watched.
examples.counter: They sat on horses galloping downhill.

cues.context: Low outward movement does not establish safety or pleasantness.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: A character or narrator perceives potential harm or coercion.

examples.positive: She heard the pursuer unlocking the door.
examples.counter: There was no danger in the empty room.

cues.context: Record whose threat assessment this is; do not treat a negated danger as present.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Awe or astonishment colours a perception or discovery.

examples.positive: The impossible city left her astonished.
examples.counter: I wonder whether the kettle is ready.

cues.context: Question-form wonder is not necessarily awe; source conventions can be ironic.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Loss or mourning is represented for a specified experiencer.

examples.positive: He mourned the friend who would not return.
examples.counter: There was no sorrow in her voice.

cues.context: Tears may also indicate joy; a funeral setting alone does not establish every viewpoint.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: A comic, playful or incongruous framing is supported by context.

examples.positive: A safe landed on the indestructible officer, who complained about the inconvenience.
examples.counter: A silent account of a fatal injury.

cues.context: Irony and deadpan understatement need context, not a fixed adjective or assumed low stakes.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Care, affection or interpersonal gentleness is foregrounded.

examples.positive: She covered his sleeping shoulders with the blanket.
examples.counter: He covered the tracks to hide the robbery.

cues.context: Identify the relationship and action; soft movement alone is insufficient.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: A previously established strain eases for an experiencer.

examples.positive: At last the alarm stopped and they breathed freely.
examples.counter: The quiet before the ambush.

cues.context: Require prior tension; silence may instead increase anticipation.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: Presentation invites a gap between literal wording and an evaluated event.

examples.positive: An excellent landing, he said from the wreckage.
examples.counter: He sincerely praised a smooth landing.

cues.context: Signals are illustrative only; positive words during harm do not prove irony.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.uncertainty: Use uncertain or abstain when text/context does not establish this label; do not force a winner.

entries.definition: A perception or feeling is situated in a particular character.

examples.positive: To her the familiar corridor seemed threatening.
examples.counter: The corridor was forty feet long.

cues.context: Store the experiencer separately; do not transfer one character feeling to every speaker.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.definition: An event is represented as remembered or recounted rather than current.

examples.positive: Yesterday, he remembered, the guards had chased him.
examples.counter: The guards were chasing him now.

cues.context: Quoted narration can contain a complete remembered scene; annotation should mark the performance scope.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.definition: An event is conditional, planned, wished or counterfactual.

examples.positive: If they followed, he would flee.
examples.counter: They followed and he fled.

cues.context: Conditional scope may cover only one clause; do not suppress actual action elsewhere.
cues.negation: Check clause scope, experiencer and event actuality; a keyword alone is insufficient.

entries.definition: The represented event is situated in the active story scene.

examples.positive: Now she crossed the bridge.
examples.counter: She described crossing it years earlier.

cues.context: Past grammatical tense can still narrate the active scene; tense alone is not actuality.

entries.definition: Physical cold or exposure is established in the setting.

examples.positive: Snow stung their faces and their hands shook.
examples.counter: His cold reply ended the conversation.

entries.definition: Protection or a sheltered interior is materially present.

examples.positive: Inside the cabin the fire warmed their hands.
examples.counter: They searched for shelter in the storm.

cues.context: Seeking protection is not attaining it; comfort and threat can coexist indoors.
